title: What Contextualization Means
brief: Define contextualization using the source's own language: the meaningful use of language for real communicative purposes, and the way language users construct language in a given context. Unpack the source's six dimensions of language learning in context — real or simulated situations, physical setting, purpose of exchange, roles of participants, socially acceptable norms, and attention to medium, tone, genre, and register — explaining what each dimension means for the classroom teacher. Close by distinguishing 'constructing language' (deciding what language to use for what purpose in a given situation to meet particular social needs) from simply memorising isolated forms, using the source's own glossary definition.

title: Why Context Matters for Language Learning
brief: Draw exclusively on the source's Module Focus bullet points to explain the three reasons the source gives for using contextualized language: that language is constructed through a blend of purpose, situation, and social needs; that a contextualized approach supports integrated skills and pair and group work; and that it can foster a deeper level of language use, especially when themes and topics are high-interest and motivate students. Explain each reason in practical terms a trainee teacher can grasp, using the source's definitions of 'integrated skills' (language skills used together for communication) and 'motivate' from the preview vocabulary. Do not make any claims about research or studies.

title: The Construction-Site Discovery Task: A Worked Example
brief: Walk through the Athens subway construction task from the source in full detail as a concrete worked example of contextualized language in action. Describe the scenario as the source presents it — a construction worker uncovering a 2,500-year-old painted bowl, then being asked to design a subway station with a museum displaying the artefacts — and explain how the debrief questions the source provides (formal or informal language? particular vocabulary? verb tenses for discovery and future plans?) reveal the language that naturally emerges from the task. Use the source's own debrief language to show that this task is communicative, engages learners in real-world scenarios, and draws on integrated language that is meaningful in context. Also note the source's extension ideas — writing a dialogue between construction workers or between an archaeologist and a reporter, and acting out the discovery including the ethical question of whether to keep the bowl — as ways to deepen the same context.

title: Themes and Topics as the Organising Principle
brief: Explain how the source recommends that teachers contextualize language instruction by organising curriculum content according to themes or topics, and that these themes work best when they are threaded throughout the course of study. Use the four classroom examples from the source's observation guide answer key to illustrate the range of themes possible — body parts, rain forest animals, television viewing habits, and genetic testing and ethics — showing how each theme determined the activities, materials, and language level in that classroom. Draw on the source's descriptions of each classroom scene (for example, the paper rain forest built in one corner, the overhead transparency prepared by students, the skit about television addiction) to make the principle concrete. Include the source's point that when students share real-world information with each other and teaching comes from them and not only from the teacher, students are more motivated to learn and listen to one another.

title: Activity Types That Build Context
brief: Survey the range of activity types the source identifies for contextualizing language, drawing on both the Module Focus list and the additional techniques list on page 18: games and interactive activities; storytelling, dramatization, and acting out language including singing and chanting; student presentations; reading and listening to authentic text; problem-solving tasks, riddles, and role-plays; projects such as bulletin boards, models, and research presentations; and use of realia and authentic materials. For each category, use the source's own classroom examples where available — for instance, the 'Head, Shoulders, Knees and Toes' song for body parts vocabulary, the rain forest song about poisonous monkeys, and the skit in which a son gives up television viewing to play soccer — to show how the activity type and the theme reinforce each other. Note the source's point that physical movement activities are good for warm-up and transition points, and that older or more advanced students can also benefit from activities with a physical dimension such as building something or leading a how-to session.

title: Building Context from Your Own Classroom
brief: Guide the trainee through the source's four-step action plan for applying contextualized language in their own teaching. Step 1: identify themes or topics already in the curriculum that students enjoy and are motivated to know more about, or ask students to help identify them. Step 2: design a portion of a lesson — the source suggests a 15-minute segment — that introduces authentic tasks, motivates students through role play, project work, problem-solving, puzzles, or imaginary settings, or reviews lesson content through a game, song, or performance. Step 3: share the plan with peers, explain what activities come before and after the segment, and gather feedback. Step 4: rewrite the design, try it with the class, and think about how to revisit key content and language concepts in later lessons. Emphasise the source's framing that teachers should apply the concepts to their own classrooms and situations, and that themes work best when threaded throughout the course of study.
